title: HTTP and REST API design
blurb: Methods, status codes, idempotency, headers, caching, versioning. The highest-value non-code topic on the whole path — it comes up in frontend, backend and fullstack interviews alike.

questions.q: Which HTTP methods are defined as idempotent?
choices: GET and HEAD only, since they are the only methods that never change state
POST and PATCH, because the server can detect and skip a repeated request
GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE: repeating one leaves the same end state
Every method at all, provided the client resends a byte-identical request body
questions.why: Idempotent means N identical requests have the same effect on the server as one. DELETE twice leaves it deleted (the second may return 404, which is fine). GET and HEAD are safe as well as idempotent; PUT and DELETE change state but idempotently. POST is not, which is why double-submits create duplicate orders.
questions.asked: Extremely common, because it explains retries, double-submits and payment bugs.

questions.q: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
choices: PUT only ever creates resources; PATCH only ever updates existing ones
PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH applies a partial change to it
PATCH is a newer alias for PUT, and servers must treat them identically
PUT is for JSON bodies; PATCH is for form-encoded bodies from HTML forms
questions.why: A PUT that omits a field should clear it, because you sent the full representation. PATCH sends only what changes, which is why "field absent" vs "field set to null" matters so much in a PATCH payload. PUT can also create a resource at a URI the client chooses.
questions.asked: A phone-screen staple; the absent-vs-null follow-up shows whether you have built a PATCH endpoint.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 401 response from a 403?
choices: 401 is for an expired token; 403 is for a request with no token at all
401 means not authenticated; 403 means authenticated but not allowed
401 is for API clients; 403 is the same error when shown to a browser
403 means the resource does not exist; 401 means it exists but is locked
questions.why: 401 (despite its name, "Unauthorized") means "who are you?" and should carry a WWW-Authenticate header; an expired token is a 401 too. 403 means logging in again will not help. Some APIs deliberately return 404 instead of 403 to avoid revealing that a resource exists.
questions.asked: Asked constantly, and easy to get right, so getting it wrong stands out.

questions.q: A request body fails validation. Which status should the API return?
choices: 500, because the server could not complete the request as sent
404, because no resource matching the submitted data exists yet
400, or 422 if you separate malformed syntax from invalid content
200 with an error field, so every client parses replies the same way
questions.why: 4xx says the client must change the request; 500 says the server failed and invites a retry. 422 is the finer-grained "valid JSON, invalid content". Returning 200 with `{ error }` breaks every generic HTTP client, retry policy and monitoring dashboard.
questions.asked: Checks you know status codes are a contract with clients and monitoring, not decoration.

questions.q: What does 409 Conflict mean in practice?
choices: The server is overloaded and rejects any new writes until its load drops
The client sent two headers whose values contradict one another
Two requests for the same resource reached the server at exactly the same moment
It clashes with current state, such as a duplicate email or a stale version
questions.why: Typical uses: registering an email that already exists, or an optimistic-concurrency failure where the resource changed since the client read it. Overload is 503 (or 429 per client), and two simultaneous requests are only a conflict if one invalidates the other.
questions.asked: Leads straight into how you detect a stale write, which is the interesting part.

questions.q: How should REST resource URLs be named?
choices: Verbs that describe the action, such as /getUserOrders?userId=42
Plural nouns with ids and shallow nesting, such as /users/42/orders
One /api endpoint that takes a command name in the request body
Whatever matches the controller's method names, so code and URL agree
questions.why: The HTTP method is the verb and the URL is the noun. Nest one level at most: `/users/42/orders/7/items/3` is worse than `/order-items/3`. A single command endpoint is RPC, which is a legitimate style but not REST.
questions.asked: A quick check that you have read and designed more than one API.

questions.q: What does a 201 Created response usually include?
choices: An empty body, since the client already has the data it just sent
The full collection, so that the client can refresh its whole list in one go
A redirect to the list page, so a browser refresh cannot resubmit
A Location header for the new resource, and often its representation
questions.why: Returning the created object gives the client the server-assigned id and timestamps without another round trip; 204 is right when there is genuinely nothing to return. Redirect-after-POST is a pattern for HTML form pages (303), not for JSON APIs.
questions.asked: Checks you think about what the client needs next, not just what the server did.

questions.q: How does offset pagination (`?page=3&limit=20`) break on a busy dataset?
choices: It cannot be combined with ORDER BY, so pages arrive in random order
Databases cap OFFSET at 1,000 rows, so deep pages return an error
Inserts and deletes between requests make rows skip or repeat across pages
It needs a total row count, which the database must recompute for every page
questions.why: If a row is inserted before page 3 while the user is on page 2, every later row shifts by one and one is shown twice. Deep offsets are also slow, because the database still walks and discards every row before the offset. Keyset pagination fixes both.
questions.asked: A great question: it needs both API design and database awareness.

questions.q: What is an ETag for?
choices: A checksum the client verifies to detect corruption of the body in transit
A version fingerprint for conditional requests: 304 on reads, 412 on stale writes
An id the server assigns each client so it can track them across requests
A label naming the API release that served the response, for debugging
questions.why: The client sends `If-None-Match` on GET and gets a bodyless 304 if nothing changed. On PUT, `If-Match` lets the server reject a write based on a stale read with 412, which is how HTTP prevents lost updates. Integrity in transit is TLS's job.
questions.asked: Few candidates know the write-side use; naming If-Match is a strong signal.

questions.q: What is the difference between `Cache-Control: no-store` and `no-cache`?
choices: no-cache forbids keeping a copy; no-store keeps one but revalidates it first
They are synonyms; no-cache is simply the HTTP/1.0 spelling of no-store
no-store applies only to shared proxies; no-cache applies only to browsers
no-store forbids keeping a copy; no-cache keeps one but revalidates it first
questions.why: The naming is genuinely backwards, which is why the swapped option is tempting. `no-store` is what you want for sensitive responses. `no-cache` is "check with me first", usually paired with an ETag so the check is cheap. The HTTP/1.0 relic is `Pragma: no-cache`.
questions.asked: A precise question that separates people who have configured caching from those who have read about it.

questions.q: How do you evolve a public API without breaking existing clients?
choices: Bump the version on every release so clients always know what changed
Add fields rather than change them; version only for breaking changes
Never change a published API; build a new one beside it per feature
Add a query parameter per change so clients opt in one at a time
questions.why: Additive changes are compatible as long as clients ignore unknown fields. Breaking changes need a new version and a migration path: run both and give consumers a deprecation window. Versioning every release forces needless migrations.
questions.asked: Checks you have maintained an API that someone else depended on.

questions.q: What should an API error response body contain?
choices: The exception message and stack trace, so client developers can debug it
A plain string message, since the status code already carries the meaning
A consistent shape: a stable code, a human message and field-level details
Nothing at all, because well-behaved clients should branch on the status code alone
questions.why: Clients need to branch on something stable, not on English prose, and forms need to know which field failed. RFC 9457 Problem Details (formerly RFC 7807: `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`) is a ready-made shape that ASP.NET Core emits by default. Stack traces belong in logs.
questions.asked: Very common for backend roles. Never leak a stack trace to a client.

questions.q: What does a 429 status mean, and what should accompany it?
choices: Request Timeout, sent with a Keep-Alive header to extend it
Payload Too Large, sent with a Content-Length header to cap it
Too Many Requests, ideally sent with a Retry-After header
Service Unavailable, sent with a Location header to redirect
questions.why: Retry-After tells the client exactly how long to back off, which turns a guess into a contract. Timeout is 408, payload too large 413 and unavailable 503. A well-behaved client honours Retry-After rather than retrying in a tight loop.
questions.asked: Checks you can name the header that makes rate limiting cooperative.

questions.q: Why is a GET endpoint with side effects a problem?
choices: GET requests cannot carry a body, so the change has no data to work with
GET responses are slower, because browsers revalidate them every time
It only breaks naming conventions; clients and proxies treat it exactly the same
Crawlers, prefetchers and caches may issue or replay GETs you never expect
questions.why: GET is defined as safe, so browsers prefetch links, crawlers follow them and retries repeat them. The classic disaster is a `/delete?id=5` link that a crawler walks. Data for a GET travels in the URL, so the lack of a body is not the problem.
questions.asked: The crawler-deleted-everything story is a favourite; it tests whether "safe" means anything to you.

questions.q: What difference between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 matters to a web developer?
choices: HTTP/2 lets the server skip status codes, as each stream signals success
HTTP/2 drops request headers and moves the metadata into the body
HTTP/2 keeps one request per connection but opens far more of them
HTTP/2 multiplexes requests over one connection, so bundling matters less
questions.why: Under HTTP/1.1 browsers opened about six connections per host and each carried one request at a time, so concatenating files and sharding domains paid off. With multiplexing, many small cacheable files can beat one big bundle. HTTP/2 also compresses headers, making cookies cheaper.
questions.asked: Checks your build and hosting habits are current rather than inherited from 2012.

questions.q: The browser sends this preflight before a cross-origin PUT. What must your server return for the PUT to go ahead?
questions.code:
OPTIONS /api/orders/7 HTTP/1.1
Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type, authorization
choices: A 204 with an Allow: PUT header, which browsers read to decide on CORS
A 401 when unauthenticated, as the preflight carries the Authorization header
A 2xx with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, -Methods and -Headers covering it
A 200 with the resource body, which the browser reuses for the real PUT
questions.why: The browser checks the Access-Control-Allow-* headers on an ok response against the method and headers it asked about, then sends the PUT. A preflight never carries credentials, so auth middleware that rejects OPTIONS with 401 is a classic cause of mystery CORS failures. `Allow` is unrelated to CORS.
questions.asked: Guaranteed if the role touches a browser and an API on different origins; the 401-on-OPTIONS bug is the follow-up.

questions.q: Where does authentication information belong in an HTTP request?
choices: A query parameter, so the token survives redirects and is easy to test
The request body, so that it is encrypted along with the payload
The Authorization header, or a cookie for browser sessions, never the URL
A custom X-Token header, since Authorization is reserved for HTTP Basic auth
questions.why: URLs end up in browser history, server and proxy logs, and Referer headers, so a token in a query string leaks to everything in the path. Under TLS the headers are encrypted exactly like the body. Authorization carries any scheme, Bearer included.
questions.asked: Checks you know where URLs leak to, which is the whole reason for the rule.

questions.q: What does "REST is stateless" actually mean?
choices: The server stores no data at all, so all application state lives in the client
Each request carries what the server needs; no session lives in memory
Responses cannot be cached, since each depends on the request state
Clients cannot use cookies, since a cookie is state between requests
questions.why: The database is state; a per-connection, in-memory conversation is what REST forbids. A session id in a cookie is fine if the session lives in a shared store. Statelessness is what lets any instance behind a load balancer serve any request.
questions.asked: A conceptual question with a very practical consequence: horizontal scaling.

questions.q: Where do filtering, sorting and search go in a REST API for a collection?
choices: A separate endpoint per filter, such as /orders/open and /orders/by-date
Request headers such as X-Filter-Status, so the URLs stay short and clean
Path segments in a fixed order, such as /orders/status/open/sort/created
Query parameters on the collection: /orders?status=open&sort=-created
questions.why: One resource, many views of it, and the URL stays bookmarkable and cacheable. Headers are invisible in links and are not part of the cache key without `Vary`. Allow-list sortable fields: user input straight into ORDER BY is an injection risk and a surprise table scan.
questions.asked: Checks you design URLs for caching and sharing, not only for your router.

questions.q: What is an idempotency key?
choices: A hash of the request body, which the server then uses as its response cache key
A client-generated id sent with a POST so the server can recognise a retry
The primary key of the created row, returned so that clients can retry
An API key scoped to a single operation that expires once it is used
questions.why: It is how payment APIs make "create a charge" safe to retry after a timeout: the server stores the key with the result and replays that result instead of charging twice. A body hash cannot tell a retry from a genuine second identical order.
questions.asked: A strong answer to "how do you stop a double charge?"

questions.q: Behind a reverse proxy, what is the difference between 502 and 503?
choices: 502: the upstream took too long; 503: the upstream returned invalid HTML
502: a proxy got a bad reply from upstream; 503: the service is refusing work
502: the app threw an unhandled exception; 503: the database is unreachable
502: the client sent a malformed request; 503: the DNS lookup failed
questions.why: 502 usually means the app behind the proxy is down or closed the connection; 503 is the app or load balancer declining work, often with Retry-After. A slow upstream is 504, and an unhandled exception in your app is a 500 that the proxy passes through.
questions.asked: Every on-call engineer has read these codes at 3am; knowing which layer each points at speeds up triage.

questions.q: A search on a collection matches nothing. What should the API return?
choices: 404, because nothing matched and the client should treat it as missing
204 No Content, since there are no items to put in a response body
200 with an empty array: the collection exists and simply has no items
400, because the filter was too narrow to match any of the rows
questions.why: 404 means the endpoint or resource does not exist; using it for an empty result forces every client to treat a normal case as an error. 204 breaks clients that always parse a JSON array. An empty list is a successful answer.
questions.asked: Tests whether you design for the client code that consumes the response.

questions.q: For a CRUD app, what is the practical trade-off between REST and GraphQL?
choices: GraphQL lets clients pick fields; REST keeps HTTP caching and the surface simple
GraphQL is faster in every case, since it always needs one round trip
REST cannot express relationships, so related data needs GraphQL to fetch
GraphQL replaces the data layer, so the server needs no ORM or SQL at all
questions.why: GraphQL solves over- and under-fetching for many different clients. It costs you URL-based HTTP caching, brings resolver N+1 risk, and needs query depth and cost limits. For one web client and a small team, REST is usually the right call.
questions.asked: An opinion question in disguise; naming the trade-offs matters more than the choice.

questions.q: Why does an internal-facing API still need rate limiting?
choices: To make billing simpler, since each request then costs a fixed amount
To cut log volume, since rejected requests are never written to logs
It does not: internal callers are trusted, so limits only add latency
So one buggy or hostile client cannot use up capacity for everyone
questions.why: Most rate-limit incidents are self-inflicted: a retry loop or a runaway batch job from a trusted service. A limit per caller turns "the whole API is down" into "one client gets 429s".
questions.asked: Checks you think of limits as capacity protection, not only as an anti-abuse feature.

questions.q: On a request, what do `Content-Type` and `Accept` each describe?
choices: They are one header, renamed between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2
Content-Type describes the body sent; Accept, what you want back
Accept is set by servers; Content-Type is only set by clients
Content-Type belongs on responses; requests describe bodies with Accept
questions.why: Forgetting `Content-Type: application/json` on a POST is why the body goes missing: the JSON parser skips a type it does not match, so in Express 5 `req.body` stays undefined (Express 4 gave `{}`). Accept drives content negotiation for the response.
questions.asked: Basic, but it explains the most common "my body is empty" bug.

questions.q: A DELETE succeeds. What should it return?
choices: 201 Created, because the deletion is recorded as a new server event
404 Not Found, to confirm the resource no longer exists after the call
302 Found, redirecting the client to the collection it was removed from
204 No Content, or 200 with a body if there is something useful to say
questions.why: A second DELETE of the same id may return 204 (idempotent view) or 404 (literal view); both are defensible, so pick one and document it. The first, successful call should not look like a failure.
questions.asked: The second-DELETE follow-up tests whether you understand idempotency is about state, not status codes.

questions.q: What does HTTPS actually protect?
choices: The server itself from attacks, since only encrypted requests reach the app
Stored data too, since TLS also encrypts the rows at rest inside the database server
Against injection, since TLS rejects any request whose payload was altered
Confidentiality and integrity in transit, plus proof of the server's identity
questions.why: TLS stops interception and tampering between client and server, and the certificate proves who the server is. An attacker can send a perfectly encrypted injection payload; what you store, log or expose afterwards is outside TLS.
questions.asked: Checks you do not treat "we use HTTPS" as a security posture.

questions.q: Your endpoint takes 4 seconds because it calls three independent services in sequence. What is the cheapest fix that keeps the response the same?
choices: Put a cache in front of the endpoint so repeat calls skip all three
Call the three services concurrently instead of one after another
Raise the client timeout so the four seconds stop causing errors
Move the work to a background job and return 202 straight away
questions.why: Three 1.3 s calls in series take 4 s; concurrently they take about 1.3 s. A cache still pays full price on every miss, a longer timeout hides the latency, and 202 changes the contract the client depends on.
questions.asked: A practical latency question: the same lesson as the Promise.all question, at the service level.

questions.q: What is a webhook?
choices: The provider calls your endpoint when an event happens, instead of polling
A script the browser runs when the page receives a push notification
A long-lived WebSocket that the provider keeps open to your server
A scheduled job that fetches changes from the provider every minute
questions.why: Your endpoint must verify the signature, respond fast (do the work asynchronously) and tolerate duplicates, because providers retry until they get a 2xx. Fetching on a schedule is polling, the thing webhooks replace.
questions.asked: Every payment or SaaS integration uses them; the retries-mean-duplicates point is what interviewers want.

questions.q: How do you choose between WebSockets, server-sent events and polling?
choices: WebSockets for everything, since SSE and polling are legacy workarounds
SSE for chat, since it is two-way; WebSockets only for file uploads
Two-way and chatty: WebSocket; server-to-client: SSE; rare updates: polling
Polling for anything live, since WebSockets always fail behind load balancers
questions.why: WebSockets cost you connection state, reconnection logic and load-balancer configuration. SSE is one-way over plain HTTP with automatic reconnect, enough for notifications or a progress feed. Polling every 30 seconds is genuinely fine for many dashboards.
questions.asked: Checks you pick the cheapest tool that meets the need instead of defaulting to WebSockets.

questions.q: You move `POST /v1/orders` to `/v2/orders`. Which redirect makes clients repeat the POST, body included, at the new URL?
choices: 301 Moved Permanently, the standard code for any permanent move
302 Found, which tells clients to repeat the exact request elsewhere
308 Permanent Redirect, which requires the method and body be kept
303 See Other, which re-sends the original body to the new URL
questions.why: Clients, browsers included, may turn a POST into a GET on 301 and 302, and 303 means "now GET this" by definition. 307 (temporary) and 308 (permanent) forbid changing the method, so the body is re-sent.
questions.asked: A detail that bites during API migrations; it shows you have read the method-preservation rules.

questions.q: A client POSTs an XML body to an endpoint that only reads JSON. Which status names the problem precisely?
choices: 406 Not Acceptable, as the server cannot accept the media format it was sent
415 Unsupported Media Type, as the body's Content-Type is not supported
422 Unprocessable Content, as the XML is well-formed but unexpected
501 Not Implemented, as the server has no XML parser installed at all
questions.why: 415 is about the request body's Content-Type. 406 is the mirror image: the server cannot produce any format listed in the request's Accept header. The names invite the swap, which is exactly why interviewers ask. 501 means the method itself is unsupported.
questions.asked: A quick precision check on content negotiation vocabulary.

questions.q: `GET /report` returns JSON or CSV depending on the Accept header, and a CDN caches it. Which response header stops the CDN serving one format to clients that asked for the other?
choices: ETag, so that the CDN can tell the JSON body apart from the CSV body
Content-Type, which caches already fold into the cache key they use
Cache-Control: public, so the CDN re-checks the format on each request
Vary: Accept, so caches keep a separate copy per Accept header value
questions.why: A cache keys on the URL unless `Vary` names request headers that also change the response. Without it, the first client's format is served to everyone. The same applies to `Accept-Encoding` (compressed vs not) and `Accept-Language`; an ETag validates a copy, it does not select one.
questions.asked: Checks you understand how caches choose a stored response, which explains a whole class of CDN bugs.

questions.q: What is a client's `Accept-Encoding: gzip, br` header asking for?
choices: A compressed response body, which the server labels with Content-Encoding
A response in a character set other than UTF-8, such as br or gzip
Encryption of the body with one of the listed ciphers, on top of TLS
Chunked transfer, so the body arrives in pieces as soon as it is ready
questions.why: The server may compress with gzip or Brotli and says which in `Content-Encoding`; JSON and HTML typically shrink by 70% or more. Character sets travel in the `charset` parameter of Content-Type, and chunking is Transfer-Encoding.
questions.asked: A junior-level check that you know the free performance win and where it is configured.

questions.q: What does designing an API contract-first with OpenAPI buy a team?
choices: The server is generated in full, so no handlers are written by hand
Runtime validation becomes unnecessary, since the spec rejects bad input
The teams agree one spec early, then generate clients, mocks and tests
Versioning becomes unnecessary, since a spec guarantees compatibility
questions.why: Frontend and backend can work in parallel against the agreed spec, with typed clients and mock servers generated from it, and CI can diff the spec to catch breaking changes. Generators produce stubs, not business logic, and the server must still validate what it receives.
questions.asked: Common in teams with separate frontend and backend developers; checks you know what the spec is for.

questions.q: A bulk endpoint creates 100 items and 3 fail validation. Which response lets the client recover cleanly?
choices: 201, since most items were created and the client can re-fetch for gaps
400 listing the three errors, while the other 97 items remain created
A per-item result list with status and errors, so it retries only failures
500, since the batch did not fully complete and the client should resend all of it
questions.why: The client needs to know exactly which items succeeded. Return per-item results (200 or 207 Multi-Status with an entry per index), or make the batch atomic and reject all of it. A 400 while 97 rows exist lies about state, and "resend it all" creates duplicates unless creation is idempotent.
questions.asked: Checks you design the failure path of a batch, which is where imports and syncs go wrong.
